1 F33 Design §10 Buildings Not answered

Should the Lantern Glare stay a realm-wide alarm, be limited to one per realm, send every guard to investigate its tile, or Alert only the guards within 4 m of it?

§5.2 budgets defence by counting wards, but a Glare Alerts every guard in the realm within about half a second, so a Keeper's budget really buys Glares. On the harness (n=400), one Glare lifts realm 3's hold from 36.2% to 78.0%, and two shut it at 99.0%. One ward that decides the outcome breaks §13.2's rule that no single layer does. The register asks for the check to run over the kits a Keeper can build, not only over the generator's mix, and that check also shows ward count is not a steady dial for any kind: three Gravity Wells hold 88.8% and six hold 32.0%.

What the build does today

sim/src/lib.rs: when a Glare fires, fire_ward (lines 2600-2606) sets revealed_until and reveal_spot, and every guard gets the near-zone fill toward the Glare's tile for 5 s (lines 1249-1257; heist.rs GLARE_REVEAL_TICKS, GLARE_BLIND_TICKS). At 67 a tick that is Alerted in about 15 ticks. The ordinary alarm already spreads by distance: guards within guard::SPREAD_METRES (4, guard.rs line 68), scaled by the sheet's AlarmRange factor, are told half a second later (lib.rs lines 3048-3067; the Whispers law sets that range to 999). The Glare ignores this reach. The harness sets every guard to ALERTED (tools/heist_harness/sim.py line 608). The generator hands out kinds in turn: Snare, Well, Glare (tools/heist_harness/island.py around lines 344-356). A Glare counts as one ward against §5.2's limits (sim/src/island.rs WARD_LIMITS line 62, checked at line 414). tools/heist_harness/test_harness.py:827 test_one_lantern_glare_outweighs_a_realm_of_other_wards pins the current behaviour.

Recommended: D, Alarm reach: guards within 4 m medium confidence

All three judges agreed on the goal: under §13.2's rule that no single layer decides outcomes, the Glare must stop being a realm-wide switch, and A and B fail that test (one Glare plus others holds 94-95%). Two judges (player experience, scope) chose the investigate-at-tile rule with a one-per-realm cap. Their case rested on the earlier draft's figures, and each named, as its main risk, that sending guards to the tile might prove stronger than the proxy that was measured. The balance judge measured the rule as written, and I reproduced it at n=400: 1 Glare holds 91.8%, and with the cap 1 Glare + 3 others holds 100%. So that dissent carries: limiting the Glare's reach to §12.17's own 4 m alarm spread is the only tested rule that turns it into a dial (1 to 3 Glares 68-77%, the generator's six 89.5% to 61.2%). It also meets what the other two judges wanted: a readable, recoverable setback, no stacking switch, and a one-line change that reuses existing spread code with no editor rule. Confidence is medium: 6 Glares still sit about 5 points above the best Glare-free kit (3 Wells, 88.8%), the harness crews know where every ward is, the 8 m alarm-4 reach is unmeasured, and realm 3 stays above its band under every option.

Three judges
  • player experience D · D, with one addition for the player: when a Glare fires, the client marks its tile as the point the guards are walking to, the same way 12.17's crack ring is drawn. A crew caught by the Glare can then see where the guards are heading and use the pull as a lure. Before this ships, measure the investigate rule as written (guards walk to the tile), not the weaker suspicion-only proxy.From the player's side, the Glare as built (option A) is a hidden tile that ends the raid. Line 5880 of the design document says the Glare is "Hidden until revealed or fired", and it triggers when a crew member comes within 2 tiles. It then Alerts every guard in the realm within about half a second. So a crew that did not scout that one tile finds out the raid is over, not that it made a mistake it could recover from. That goes against §12.17 ("nothing here is random: a player who scouts an island can predict exactly what will happen") and §1.2's pillar ("Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats."). In a 20-minute session, an instant loss the player could not see coming is the most frustrating kind of failure. Option B stops a Keeper stacking Glares, but it keeps the switch. On the harness, one Glare plus five other wards holds realm 3 at 96.2%, so one hidden tile still decides the raid, and the player feels exactly what they feel under A. Option C turns the Glare into the kind of setback a heist story is made of. The alarm goes off, every guard walks to that spot, and a crew that moves during the 2-second blind can slip away or use the empty rooms. §12.17's Investigating row ("Walks to the spot and searches nearby for ten seconds, twenty from alarm level 3") already spells out behaviour the player can read. But C alone still lets a Keeper stack Glares: 2 hold 88.8% and 3 hold 97.5%. A realm full of Glares plays as a minefield, a raid ended by an early misstep, and it breaks §13.2's "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration." Option D keeps C's readable, recoverable effect and caps the Glare at one per realm. The cap is also something the player can scout: a crew knows there is at most one Glare to find. The best kit with a Glare (71.2%) lands level with the best kit without one (67.5%), inside the ±5-point standard error at n=80, so a Keeper chooses among kinds rather than buying one decisive ward. That fits §1.2's rule that wins come from reading an island's rules, not from bigger stats. The build cost is small: one effect line in sim/src/lib.rs, one check in island.rs check(), and the matching lines in the harness. That suits one-developer scope. Confidence is medium. The harness crews know where every ward is. The investigate rule that was measured is weaker than the one written. And realm 3 still holds above its 30–45% band under every option, so §5.2's ward counts need re-measuring over the kits a Keeper can build. Quotes checked with grep -F, one line each: - §10.3, line 5877: "Shows the crew to every guard in the realm for 5 seconds and blinds them for 2. No damage." - §5.2, line 762: "Each realm level now gets the smaller of the wards it needs to reach its hold band (13.2) and eight, the legibility cap 13.2 sets: 8, 8, 6, 7 and 8." - §13.2, line 7489: "If one layer decides outcomes, the others are decoration." - §1.2, line 194: "Heists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats." - §12.17, line 7153: "nothing here is random: a player who scouts an island can predict exactly what will happen" - §12.17, line 7227: "Walks to the spot and searches nearby for ten seconds, twenty from alarm level 3"
  • balance and economy C · Change the Glare's reach, not the state it sets. The Glare Alerts only the guards within 4 m of its tile. That is §12.17's own alarm spread ("guards within four metres start investigating half a second later"), and 8 m from alarm level 4. Guards still go to Alerted, the crew is still blinded 2 s, a Glare still counts as one ward, and there is no per-realm limit. Drop C's "every guard in the realm goes to Investigating and heads for the Glare's tile": measured, that rule is stronger than today's Glare, not weaker. §10.3 cell: "Shows the crew to every guard within 4 m of it for 5 seconds (8 m from alarm level 4, 12.17) and blinds the crew for 2. No damage." Build: in sim/src/lib.rs lines 1249-1257, apply the reveal only to guards within 4 tiles of reveal_spot; in tools/heist_harness/sim.py line 608, add the same distance test; update the tests and golden replays.I re-ran the harness at n=400 a cell, with the brief's settings: realm 3, 2 posts, one geometry band, three realms crossed, crack noise off, competent crew, defensive laws, v3.4 rules. The standard error is about ±2.5 points near 50% and ±1.5 near 90%. The harness copy and driver are in scratchpad/brief/f33j (run.py; GLARE_MODE in tools/heist_harness/sim.py). 1. The draft's C and D rest on the wrong measurement. The rule they describe, with every guard going to Investigating and walking to the Glare's tile, makes the Glare stronger than today: - 1 Glare holds 91.8% against the build reading's 78.0%. - 2 Glares hold 99.8%. - The generator's six hold 99.2% against 89.5%. - D's best allowed kit (1 Glare + 3 others) holds 100%. The draft's 57.5% came from raising suspicion to 600 with no destination, which is not what §12.17's Investigating does ("Walks to the spot"). What makes a Glare decisive is pointing every guard in the realm at a tile on the crew's route. Whether they arrive Alerted or Investigating barely matters. 2 F35 Design §12 Heists Not answered

How far away is cracking the Vault heard: at 5 m with the 5-second call as built, at 5 m per hit with the call deleted as brief 37's rule now ends, only by a guard beside the Vault (1 m), or by no guard at all (0 m)?

Brief 37's rule, run exactly as §32.9 writes it, finds no reach from 1 m to the Heart's 12 m that passes either of its tests, and the ten-second whole-Heart call fails too. That is because even with no call at all, holds are already 72 to 100%, far above §13.2's bands, and depth across two or more realms is already under 35 points. So the rule ends by deleting the call on evidence that says nothing about the call. Meanwhile the 5 m that v3.4 ships cuts the optimal crew's lead from +42 to +4 points. §12.17 still says 5 m is what 'the harness measured as passing the depth gate', and §32.9's row calls it 'the noise-off case (… 58 to 82 points)'. On today's harness neither is true.

What the build does today

sim/src/heist.rs:26-31 sets CRACK_NOISE_TICKS = 5 s and CRACK_REACH_METRES = 5. sim/src/lib.rs:2222-2248: from 5 s after the Vault's first hit until the Vault opens, even if cracking stops, every 5 s each awake guard within 5 walking-path steps that is not already above Investigating is put into Investigating at the Vault. Each hit is also a Sound::Breaking, 5 m before surface and law scaling (lib.rs:1840-1883, noise.rs:51). tools/heist_harness/report.py:143-195 (depth --sweep crack_reach) runs brief 37 as written and prints 'the rule as written deletes the timed call'. The harness has no per-hit hearing (sim.py:759-813 models only the call), so its 5 m row stands in for the design's no-call case.

Recommended: D, No guard hears the Vault, 0 m medium confidence

Pick D: no guard hears a hit on the Vault. A and B leave the optimal crew about +4 to +8 ahead at the Vault, which §19.27 calls making 'the systems are decoration'. D is the only setting that passes the one-realm gate: +42.0 ± 4.0, n=200. C is the close second: +33.0 ± 3.9 (gated +33.5), 2 points under 35 and inside one standard error of it, but 9 points below D, with the optimal crew losing 23 paired runs and gaining 3 (p < 0.001). The panel split. The player-experience and scope judges chose C, to keep a guard posted beside the Vault as a lever for defenders. The balance judge chose D. The recommendation goes with D for three reasons. The player judge's own fallback is met: 1 m came out clearly under the no-call result, and that judge said the Vault should then be heard by no guard. The scope judge's reason for C was build risk, and D is less code: delete the call block and its constants, and drop Task::Crack from the breaking match; the harness already models it exactly. And the defender lever C keeps is not needed now, because holds already run 72-100% with no call at all, above §13.2's bands. If F33 and F34 bring holds into band and the Vault then proves too easy, C can be put back at 1 m, and the harness already measures it. Confidence is medium. The panel went two to one the other way, C is a near miss rather than a clear failure, and depth across two or more realms still fails at any reach (+24.5 at two realms with no call).

The realm alarm stays the pressure device. I checked the sim, and in play the 5 m call adds almost nothing on top of per-hit hearing. lib.rs:1946-1952 puts any guard that hears a Sound::Breaking straight into Investigating, and a hit lands every 0.8 s, heard at 5 m (noise.rs Breaking = 10 half-metres). 3 F37 Design §14 Progression and pacing Not answered

Where does a player who never raids get the experience and pages that let them progress?

§14.4 promises that a non-raider restores the launch 24 laws in about 80 days and the full Codex in about 195, from the Library alone. Under the document's own gates, that player earns almost nothing. The Library opens at Keeper 4. Experience from spending is capped by the Spire, which Keeper levels gate. Experience from restoring laws needs pages. In the model the non-raider stalls at Keeper 2. That makes two claims false today: §10.4's claim that the Library is 'the whole of a non-raider's progression' (the floor §14.4 says 13.3 rests on), and §7.6's promise that raiding is 'not the only' path. Even without the gates, §10.4's school rule caps the Library at 12 of the launch 24. The model also leaves out §14.4's 3 pages for a Lab experiment that finds nothing. A non-raider can reach that source without a heist, and pages are how a non-raider earns experience.

What the build does today

The server grants no Keeper experience; progression exists only in the economy model. tools/economy_model/data.py:286 defines the never_raids archetype (5 sessions, 0 heists, 3 Lab experiments). model.py pages_today() (lines 579-595) gives it the Library alone. Its docstring says Lab experiments that find nothing and first meetings with a law are left out. Run for 400 days, the archetype ends at Keeper 2 (reached on day 3) with the 3 starting laws, because it never reaches the Library's Keeper 4 gate. test_economy_model.py (around line 411) asserts it stays below Keeper 12 and never restores the Codex. docs/design/generated/pacing.md prints 'never (F37)' for both Codex rows.

Recommended: B, Library plus daily goals; launch 24 is the ceiling medium confidence

B, with the tutorial's two ruins paying successful-heist experience and daily-goal pages going to the law the player is working on. This makes §14.4's launch promise true (the launch 24 in about 76–78 days against the stated 80) using systems §14.6 and §7.6 already have. Ruins are counted apart from §14.1's raids, so they never use up one of G20 C's 20 paid raids; the cost is that the tutorial ruins move the published tables by about a day. It adds one testable assertion, which suits one-developer scope. The player-experience and scope judges both chose B. The player-experience judge added the tutorial-ruin experience so the non-raider plateaus on a fresh bar at Keeper 11 with Spire 3 open, not frozen at 937 of 1,020 XP. That judge also had §14.1's counts include ruins; the brief does not, because G20 C's 20-raid week is built on §14.1's four raids. The scope judge added the page routing and the test. The balance judge dissented for C at the foiled-heist rate, correctly showing that no page source moves B's plateau past Keeper 8. That leaves chapter 3, season laws and §14.4's 195-day Codex out of a non-raider's reach, and §32's Library-output trigger cannot fix it. It stays the upgrade path if the owner wants non-raiders to reach the full Codex (day 175, raiding still about twice as fast). Confidence is medium because the dissent concerns what the floor is for, not a factual error.

What should the entry fee be keyed to, now that 2% of a saving player's Starlight costs more than raids bring in?

§14.1's player saves for the next Spire level, and the last three Spire levels cost 249,400, 548,800 and 1,207,300. A fee of 2% of what the player holds therefore grows to 14,000–24,000 a raid while hauls pay a few thousand. By §9.6's own test (a raid that pays less than staying home is skipped), a saving player should stop raiding, which neither the model nor the pacing tables assume. The raid-worth check also leaves the fee out.

What the build does today

server/src/economy.mjs entryFee() (line 158) charges min(clamp(2% × held Starlight, 100, 25,000), held). server/src/service.mjs grant() (line 564) computes it at line 580 (none for a Trace, a friendly heist or a challenge), debits it at line 581, and returns it only after a clean heist (lines 618–619). The economy model's entry_fees() (tools/economy_model/model.py line 683) charges the same and keeps (1 − success rate × 0.35) of it. rerun.CHOICES shows that removing the fee moves Keeper 40 from day 357 to day 318.

Recommended: B, 2% of B(V) at the target medium confidence

Keying the fee to the target's B(V) makes the stake proportional to what the raid can pay, so saving the way §14.1's player does is no longer punished, and kept fees stay a fixed share of raid Starlight from day 31 at every Vault level: about 20% at the lower edge and 14% at the upper with C41's recommended return rule (32% and 23% if only a clean heist returns it). C gives nearly the same pacing (Keeper 40 on day 319–326 against 315–321, both with C41 B) but still charges a saver by holdings in the mid game: at the lower edge its kept fees are 0.76× raid Starlight on day 91 (1.34× with clean-only return). D is faster still but removes the raider's stake altogether. The cost falls on defenders: the fee a foiled raider passes on drops from up to 25,000 to 48–1,845, so the defence share (5% rising to 20%, §13.1) becomes the main defence reward and is the lever to raise if §13.1's 'Defenders are paid best' needs more. It is a one-line formula change, and the raider sees the fee before choosing a target.

Also needed C41's return rule, which sets the kept share (this entry's figures assume C41 B, with clean-only figures alongside). Whether the kept fee counts in §9.6's raid-worth check (the register's recommendation); counting it moves F36's base.

What the build does today

The server treats Starglass as a currency. server/src/shop.mjs keeps it in the ledger in hundredths of a euro (1 Starglass = €1 = 100 units) and sells five packs (starglass-1, -5, -10, -20, -50). The €1 and €50 ends come from §22.1 through tools/design_facts.py STARGLASS_PACKS_EUR; the €5, €10 and €20 packs are shop.mjs's own. A purchase intent enforces §20.2's €25 and €50 monthly caps, counted in each pack's euro list price, before the store is asked; a store receipt that arrives with no intent (a restore, a family approval) is still honoured. The monthly summary is reported in 'EUR'. Starglass buys cosmetics from src/cosmetics.json (empty, D64) and the premium track at PREMIUM_PRICE = 600 (server/src/track.mjs). The free track gives 25 units at tiers 10, 20, 30 and 40, one Starglass a season. Receipts are checked by stores.mjs receipts(), which server/src/main.mjs wires in as verifyReceipt. App Store transactions are checked against pinned Apple roots (RULEBORN_STOREKIT_ROOTS, RULEBORN_BUNDLE_ID). Play purchases are checked against the licence key and consumed through googleapi.mjs (RULEBORN_PLAY_PACKAGE, RULEBORN_PLAY_LICENCE_KEY, RULEBORN_PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT). A store left unconfigured refuses every receipt. The client has no shop screen.

Recommended: C, No currency: every item priced in money medium confidence

§19.12 refuses soft-currency pricing on the evidence of [156], §27.2 records the decision as 'Every cosmetic priced in real money', and §22.1 promises every price in real money before purchase. C follows that evidence furthest, but it does not leave §19.12 untouched: the row's own remedy keeps Starglass as a season-pass wrapper at 1:1, and C rewrites that sentence, and §27.2's, to a gift wrapper only. B can show local prices too, but only by keeping a currency and deriving a rate for each store; C is the only option under which the money-illusion rule holds with no currency and no rate, and it removes G32's negative balances. Under every option: whether §20.2's €25 and €50 caps count each product's euro list price or the local amount charged, and in what currency the monthly summary is shown (shop.mjs today: euro list price, 'EUR').

18 G23 Significant §7 Laws Not answered

Where the launch law sheets in §7.7 stop short, should the rules be the simulation's readings as built, those readings with Delay's promised weakness made real, or rules you write yourself?

The server re-simulates every heist (§24.7), so whatever sim/ reads is the rule every replay is judged by, whatever the sheet says. Under those readings two sheets promise things the build does not do. Delay's weakness, "Your own guards react late too", is not a rule anywhere, so Delay has no weakness. Bounce's raider and defender lines need a character to rebound, which happens only under Pinball (Frictionless + Bounce), so Bounce alone just returns half a blow to whoever strikes a ward. Aurora's single two-row band lights a tile only 12.5 to 16.7% of the time, so in practice it mostly halves vision, like Glowing dark. Density is a separate case: §11.2 makes four ruleborn small, but sim/ plays roles, not ruleborn, so nobody is small in the build. That is a gap in the build, not a reading to adopt.

What the build does today

sim/ applies all 24 launch laws, and each reading sits beside its code in sim/src/lib.rs. Frictionless: only the crew slides; guards do not; a Halt stops a slide and the grid edge ends it (slide_on, line 3217). Bounce: a character rebounds only while sliding, so only under Pinball, off every wall. Bounce alone just returns 50% of a blow on a ward to the striker, and a Warden absorbs both (around lines 2361-2365). Density: the Warden counts as large and every other role as standard, so nobody is small, because the simulation's crew and guards are roles, not ruleborn (by_size, line 256; Role::size, line 280). Delay: holds ward effects only (queue `delayed`, lines 2480-2484 and 2555-2559); guards react on time. Aurora: one band 2 rows deep (heist.rs AURORA_BAND_ROWS) sweeps north to south once per 10 s period (in_band, line 1463). Chain lightning: jumps to the nearest standing member of the struck side within 3 tiles; a jump never jumps again, and hits on structures do not jump (chain_from, line 2775). Static: a charge builds after 5 tiles; a touch means the same or an adjacent tile; the stun lands on the nearest body, ally or not (static_touches, line 1693). Echoes: the return happens at once, where the character fell, after its loot has dropped. Soul swap: once per character; the one swapping takes none of the blow; only a hit sets it off (soul_swap, line 2669). Thorns: a touch means standing on or beside a wall or a live Thorn Hedge, costing 5% of full health once a second, and the Vault and pylons do not count (thorns, line 2832). Each reading is held by a test in sim/src/tests.rs. sim/ plays every law at its tier I figure.

Recommended: B, Keep readings; Delay slows guards too medium confidence

§7.7 sets the bar: a law without a weakness does not ship, and under the build's reading Delay has none. The document already assumes Delay slows reactions: its sheet says 'Characters flinch a beat late', and §11.3's Clear-headed trait and Hourkeeper's resist make characters immune to it, which only matters if Delay does more than hold wards. B keeps the other tested readings, costs one queued state change, and makes the written sheet match the rule the server replays.

Also needed Under any option: Density's weakness line, 'Your Breakers become slow targets.', is false by §11.2's own roster (no Breaker is large, and Emberling, a Breaker, is small); it should read 'Your Wardens become slow targets.' sim/ must carry each crew member's and guard's ruleborn Size (§11.2) in place of Role::size (sim/src/lib.rs line 280) before Density's small band plays. Also decide whether Bounce alone passes §7.7's both-sides test, since without Frictionless it only returns half a blow to whoever strikes a ward. Under A, a new weakness sentence for Delay.

Weigh with G25, G24, G36

  • §7.7 Your own guards react late too.
  • §7.7 Characters flinch a beat late; effects land after a pause.
  • §11.3 Clear-headed: immune to Spores and Delay.
  • §7.7 Bands of light sweep the realm every 10 seconds. Inside a band everyone can be seen from twice as far; between bands, vision halves.

One row holds three different rules: Regrowth heals what is still standing, Bloom and Crystal growth regrow broken things after a set time, and Tidemark rolls broken things back to a mark. That is the fault §7.3 says version 2 of the sheet fixed for Drain and for Healing and regrowth: one name for several rules. §7.3's combining rule covers only multipliers and on/off values, so a time has no stated way to combine. The build therefore multiplies times like any other number: Bloom and Crystal growth together regrow a hedge after 51.2 s, far slower than either law alone.

sim/ keeps the heal as Param::StructureRegrowth (Regrowth, 2%/s) and the timer as Param::RegrowSeconds (Bloom 10 s, Crystal growth 8 s; sim/src/laws_table.rs lines 74, 97, 103). The timer applies only to broken Thorn Hedges (sim/src/lib.rs, around lines 2378-2402), so Crystal growth's walls and its 'clear crystal' do not exist. Every value, times included, combines by multiplication in Sheet::apply (sim/src/lib.rs line 115, called from refresh_sheet, line 1181). refresh_sheet applies the standing laws in weave order, the order the island lists them (World::weave, line 830), with no layer or school sort. A scratch test on a copy of sim/ that wove both laws gave 1,536 ticks = 51.2 s: 10 s × 8 s, each cut a fifth by the Bloom harmony both laws carry (harmonised, line 152). Tidemark is `simulated: false` (laws_table.rs line 88). Crystal growth and Tidemark are not launch laws, so at launch only Bloom sets a time.

§7.3 split Drain and Healing and regrowth for exactly this reason, and says a split is free while nothing has shipped; after launch it would pin replays. The build already keeps two parameters, so the code change is one combining rule on one parameter.

Which figures should §18.6, §18.7 and §20.12 give the Workshop: the server's current ones, the same rules with a larger quota and larger word lists, or no figures in the document at all?

The server already enforces the Workshop with figures the document never gives: how many islands a player may publish, how much storage they get, what 'cleared' means, what a player can report an island for, what a completion 'spike' is, and whether a remix earns its original anything. If nobody decides, the build's guesses become the game's rules without review. Four of them are visible to players: the name pool, the slot count, the report reasons, and the quota when it refuses a publish. Two of the build's figures hurt the creators §18.7 rewards: the quota is a lifetime cap, and the name pool produces duplicate names almost at once.

What the build does today

server/src/workshop.mjs holds each reading as a named constant with a test (server/test/workshop.test.mjs). Names: an adjective plus a noun from server/src/words.json, 16 × 16 = 256 names, in English and Brazilian Portuguese (workshop.mjs:22, 76-81). Constellation names come from the same lists (social.mjs found(), lines 58-61; D63). Slots: SLOTS = 5, and BUILDER_SLOTS = 3 more for §18.7's Builder, so 8 (workshop.mjs:30-31). Quota: QUOTA_BYTES = 64 KiB, summed over every island the creator ever published, withdrawn and removed ones included, because nothing is deleted. A withdrawn island frees its slot, but its bytes still count (workshop.mjs:36, 133-139). Cleared: the creator's re-simulated replay gets any grade but foiled and banks loot (workshop.mjs:64-66). Report reasons: unfair, unplayable, copied, offensive, other (workshop.mjs:58). Spike: at least 50 completions in a day and more than 5 times the island's daily mean over the week before; the island is flagged and queued for a person (workshop.mjs:50-51, spike()). Remix: the new island names its original (remix_of) and earns the original nothing.

Recommended: B, Build's rules, figures that don't bite medium confidence

The build's rules are sensible, enforced and tested, and writing them into the document keeps it the source of truth, which suits one-developer scope. But two of its figures work against the players §18.7's ladder is meant to reward. A 64 KiB lifetime quota locks a creator out after about 133 publishes, and 256 names shared with constellations produce a duplicate by about the 19th island. Raising the quota to 1 MiB and the lists to 64 × 64 are data changes, and the worst-case storage bill stays about $16 a month, so §20.12's cost control holds.

How do a database restore and §24.6's table exports keep deletions made after they were taken, and where does the deletion log live?

§24.6 names two copies of the database: a point-in-time restore to any minute in the last 30 days, and "an export of every table kept elsewhere" for leaving the vendor. Restoring to a minute before a deletion brings back the identity, push token, telemetry and friendships, and removes the record that the deletion happened. An export made before a deletion holds the same data for as long as it is kept, and nothing limits its age. Both break §20.12's "backups included" promise, and nobody would know.

What the build does today

server/src/accounts.mjs. Journal.append writes each deletion (account id, reason, time; nothing that names a person) to a local file with fsync before the deletion's transaction (accounts.mjs:44-70). reapplyDeletions() makes again every journalled deletion the database does not hold. main.mjs:169-176, the node:http server, runs it at every start, before the listener accepts sign-ins. The edge handler (http.mjs) never calls it. The journal path is RULEBORN_DELETIONS. By default it is server/.data/deletions.jsonl, the same directory as the database. privacy.json keeps the journal for good as §20.12's log. server/test/privacy.test.mjs restores a copy from before two deletions and checks both are made again. No table export is built.

Recommended: D, Object-storage journal, re-applied at start within the restore window medium confidence

It keeps A's automatic re-apply, which holds even when nobody remembers a step, the reason §24.6 gives for automatic restore. A as built needs a local file, which the edge functions §24.1 names do not have, and its start-time cost grows with every deletion ever made. Bounding the re-apply to the 30-day restore window keeps each start to one month's deletions for a one-developer operation. A 30-day limit on exports makes "backups included" true for both copies §24.6 keeps.

Also needed Where the journal lives in the real deployment (which bucket or store, and who can write to it). Legal confirmation that keeping account ids in the log for good is acceptable. If F43 B is chosen, each journal entry must also record the player's withdraw choice.

31 G21 Minor §24 Technical logic Not answered

What is one target list's 'difficulty band', and how often are the lists rebuilt?

§24.8 makes target selection a cached file 'per difficulty band', 'generated periodically', and defines neither. The band decides how big each file is and what the device must filter itself. The rebuild period decides how long a republished island's old snapshot stays offered, and how many database rows every rebuild reads. In this build that read count grows through each season (see G33).

What the build does today

server/src/service.mjs targetLists() (line 214) builds one list per realm level ('realm-level-N', or the snapshot's own band column when set). Each entry carries the island's Glicko rating and deviation, Keeper level and Renown, so the device applies §12.22's filters itself. A new player's islands are left off the lists while their shield holds (matchmaking.mjs shielded(): their first 72 hours or until their first raid). Lists are content-addressed, so an unchanged band keeps its edge cache. A band keeps its current and previous list, and a band with no islands left loses its list. server/src/main.mjs:181-184 rebuilds every 15 minutes (TARGET_LISTS_MS) and once at start. A lease on a snapshot no island holds any more is granted as an echo (§12.3) for 14 days after it was published: the raider is paid a haul, but no Renown moves, and the owner is not paid, rated or notified. After 14 days, and always for a trace or a friendly heist, it is refused as 'superseded' (service.mjs:346-365, 626-653). For each listed island a rebuild calls seasons.league(owner), which re-sums every Renown row the owner has this season (renownIn(), seasons.mjs:109-115).

Recommended: B, Realm level, rebuilt hourly medium confidence

Realm level is the unit of §12.22's guarantee, and the build already carries ratings so the device can filter, so the band should stay as built. Hourly rebuilds cut the rows that rebuilds read fourfold, and players see little of the cost: a new player is shielded anyway, and a stale entry is played as an echo that pays a haul and takes nothing from its owner. That fits §24.1's goal that the free tier carries the early game. Separately, and needing no decision, the build should keep each player's season Renown as a running total on the standing row. That is the larger saving: about 7 reads per island per rebuild instead of up to about 230 at mid-season.

Also needed For C, a rating band width in Glicko-2 points.

Weigh with G33

38 G32 Minor §20 Wellbeing, safety, age Not answered

When a store refunds a purchase after its Starglass was granted, what does the server take back, and can a Starglass balance go below zero?

A player can buy Starglass, spend it on a cosmetic or the premium track, then get a refund from Apple or Google. As built, they keep everything. Refunds already granted cannot be taken back until someone decides how. §20.2's monthly caps for minors also count every purchase, refunded or not. How fresh a sign-in proof must be is written nowhere in the document, only in stores.mjs.

What the build does today

Proofs, all in server/src/stores.mjs. A Game Center signature must be within 5 minutes of the server clock (GAME_CENTER_FRESH_MS, :36, checked :234) under a pinned root. A Google ID token is accepted until its own exp plus 5 minutes of clock skew, and its iat may not be more than 5 minutes ahead (GOOGLE_SKEW_MS :304, :403-404); nothing bounds its age otherwise. A StoreKit 2 transaction must chain to its pinned root, match the app, be unrevoked and come from Production; Sandbox is accepted only if the operator sets RULEBORN_APPLE_SANDBOX=1 (stores.mjs:138-139, main.mjs:68). A Play purchase must be purchaseState 0, and is looked up and consumed before grant (googleapi.mjs). A purchase intent is held 15 minutes (shop.mjs:30), and the session token lasts 60 minutes (tokens.mjs:16). Refunds after a grant are not handled (D67): no App Store Server Notifications and no Play voided-purchases check. The balance is the sum of ledger rows (service.mjs:707). spendStarglass refuses when the balance is below the cost (service.mjs:727). It is called for cosmetics (shop.mjs:210) and the premium track (track.mjs:173). The schema does not stop a negative sum.

Recommended: B, Claw back in full; balance may go negative medium confidence

Money never buys power (§22), so the fairness question is only whether refunds become free items. A negative balance closes that loop with one append-only ledger row and never takes a worn item away. That is the smallest build for one developer, and it keeps §24.12's single-ledger rule.

Also needed Further decisions: whether a refunded purchase still counts against a minor's monthly cap (the build counts it); whether the proof windows are accepted (Game Center five minutes, Google token expiry plus five minutes); the Android identity question in D67 (Google account or Play Games player). Under §19.12 Starglass is also a gift wrapper, so the rule must say whose balance a refunded gift is taken from (the giver's, under B). And whether the server answers Apple's CONSUMPTION_REQUEST notifications with consumption information, which can lower refund approvals for spent Starglass under any option.

  • §22.1 Starglass, in packs from about €1 to €50
  • §20.2 Family approval where set up; €25 a month cap
  • §22 Money buys looks and a season pass. It never buys power, speed or chance.

39 G29 Minor §20 Wellbeing, safety, age Not answered

Which telemetry definitions should the document adopt: what counts as a session, how long raw events are kept within 30 to 90 days, and whether the monthly survey is a monthly sample or a monthly ask?

The targets that open chapter 25 are read from these events, and nothing defines their unit. They are session length of 5 to 9 minutes, 3 to 6 sessions a day for active players, players still playing after 1, 7, 30 and 60 days, the "chore" share and the worth-your-time average. §25.3's crash-free share and absence warning are read from the same events. The build counts every sign-in as a session, so how many sessions one sitting makes depends on when the client signs in again, which it must do at least once an hour. The build also cannot report two of chapter 25's targets: 60-day retention and the chore share. §24's "monthly survey" and §25.4's "never more than once a quarter per player" disagree unless someone says how they fit together.

What the build does today

server/src/telemetry.mjs and service.mjs. A "session" event is written on every POST /v1/session (service.mjs:145), and write() adds the player to first_seen on that event (telemetry.mjs:118-119). A token lasts 60 minutes (tokens.mjs:16, SESSION_MS). The server does not limit sign-ins. The client keeps the token only in memory (client/scripts/server_client.gd:9, 50) and must sign in again at least once an hour of continuous play. report() gives a raw session count and the crash-free share. It computes no session length: session_end seconds are stored but used only for the crash-free share (telemetry.mjs:244, 265). Raw events are kept 90 days (RAW_DAYS = facts.RAW_KEEP_DAYS[1]). A daily compact() then keeps only daily counts and, once a cohort is 31 days old, its day-1, day-7 and day-30 returns. The cohorts table has no day-60 column. The server accepts at most one survey per player per 90 days, counted from when it received the last one (SURVEY_GAP_MS, telemetry.mjs:32, 161-163). It has no sampler: who is asked is up to the client. The survey event is exactly 11 answers, each 1 to 7. The "worth" rating is 1 to 5, capped at 24 a day like session_end, and report() weighs each player once, by their own average. A batch holds at most 100 events dated no more than 7 days back (BATCH, LATE_MS). The pseudonym is an HMAC of the account. The client sends no telemetry yet.

40 G38 Minor §20 Wellbeing, safety, age Not answered

How long is something that names a player kept once it is closed (a sent notification, a used or lapsed friend invite, an expired challenge link, a superseded target list, a lapsed purchase intent, a lease that expired unplayed)?

§24.3 limits only raw replays and logs, and §20.5 says to collect only what is needed. Without a rule, closed records grow for good. The store declarations (declarations.md) must state how long each is kept. Target lists are public objects that name every candidate's account id.

What the build does today

server/src/main.mjs runs tidy() at start and then daily (main.mjs:247-252), and the stored limits are declared in server/privacy.json. A sent notification is deleted 7 days after it was sent (notifications.mjs:29, SENT_KEEP_DAYS; the reminder check reads 3 days back). A used friend invite is deleted at the next daily tidy, an unused one after 7 days, and a challenge link after 7 days (friends.mjs:20-21, 118-124). Target lists are remade every 15 minutes and once at start (main.mjs:182-184, TARGET_LISTS_MS). Each band keeps its current list and the one before. The one before moves only when the band's list changes: a rebuild that produces the same bytes keeps the same hash and deletes nothing, so a superseded list is deleted when its band's list next changes, at least one rebuild later and with no upper limit in a quiet band (service.mjs:246-266). A band with no islands left loses both its lists (service.mjs:270-276). An under-13 deletion remakes the lists at once with no previous list (accounts.mjs:189). sweepLists() at start removes lists no band names (main.mjs:178). Lists are served through GET /v1/bundles with "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" (http.mjs:326), so an edge or device cache may hold a deleted list for up to a year. Purchase intents (held 15 minutes, shop.mjs:30) and leases are kept for good as records (privacy.json), including intents never redeemed and leases that expired still open; only an under-13 player's open leases are deleted. server/test/privacy.test.mjs runs each limit.

Recommended: B, One rule: closed things go within 7 days medium confidence

One rule matches §20.5's "collect only what's needed", covers features the document has not built yet, and costs a single-developer project nothing to keep true. Applying it finds three gaps in the build: lapsed purchase intents and unplayed leases kept for good, target lists cached for a year where they should last no longer than one rebuild interval (an hour under G21 B), and a superseded list kept at origin until its band changes, which in a quiet band is never. All are small fixes.

Also needed A cache purge on deletion: a shorter max-age does not recall copies already cached. An under-13 erasure (F43) must purge the erased island bundles, and ideally the superseded lists, from the edge cache, because http.mjs:326 serves every object under /v1/bundles immutable for a year.

Weigh with G21, G29, F43, F50

What the document says
  • §20.5 Collect only what's needed to run the game; no advertising identifiers; analytics are pseudonymous.
  • §24.3 Short retention. Raw replays and logs are kept 30 to 90 days, long enough for validation and analysis, then aggregated and discarded.
  • §24.8 Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
  • §24.1 Immutable, content-addressed island bundles on zero-egress object storage, cached at the edge for a year

42 G34 Minor §13 Defence Not answered

Should raids against a player be gathered into fewer notifications, and may a player set their daily reminder inside their night?

§14.6 lists what may be sent and §20.2 sets the quiet hours. Nothing says how many raid messages a player gets, what happens to a reminder set for 23:00, or whose clock the night is measured on. §30.5 records that three to six pushes a week lead about 40% of users to turn notifications off. How often raid messages go out therefore decides whether players keep notifications on at all.

What the build does today

server/src/notifications.mjs. The clock is the player's own: the device reports an offset from UTC in minutes (set(), ±14 hours). The default is 0 (db.mjs line 49), so a device that never reports gets UTC nights, and a daylight-saving change needs a new report. raided() adds a raid to an unsent 'raided' message if one is waiting. main.mjs line 260 delivers every minute, so in practice the raids of one night become one morning message, and each daytime raid is its own message. remind() queues the chosen daily reminder, and a time inside the night is held by due() until the night ends (08:00). The server sends the kind with its data fields ({kind, ...data}) and the device words it. Nights come from facts.json NIGHT_HOURS: 21–8 for 13-15, 22–8 for 16-17 and adults. Only an adult can open the night; under 18, set() refuses with the_night_is_always_quiet_under_18. deliver() checks the night again when it sends. The client reports neither an offset nor a push token yet.

Recommended: C, One message a day for raids medium confidence

§14.6 names "a heist against you" as a notification worth sending, and §14.10 rules out escalating notifications, so raids should notify but rarely. §17.8 says a raid takes nothing, so a day's delay costs the defender nothing, and one daily message cuts server pushes from about 12 to 19 a week to at most 7 (about 6 for players with no reminder). That is still at or above the three to six a week that §30.5 links to about 40% turning notifications off, and the device's own timers add more, so the push count should be measured in the beta, with D as the fallback if opt-outs run high. Refusing reminders inside the night keeps §20.2's night clean, and the change stays inside notifications.mjs.

Also needed The clock must be settled under every option. The build stores a fixed offset with a default of 0 (db.mjs line 49). With that default a 13-to-15 in Brazil (UTC−3) gets pushes from 05:00 local, inside §20.2's "Never, 21:00 to 08:00", and a daylight-saving change moves a minor's night by an hour until the device reports again. Proposed rule: the device sends its IANA time zone (e.g. America/Sao_Paulo) with the push token and on every launch, the server works out the night from that zone, and no push goes to an account that has not reported one. That is one column and one check in notifications.mjs set() and due().

Weigh with G35, F48, D68

What the document says
  • §14.6 Notifications: only for things the player can act on (storage full, a character rested, an experiment finished, a heist against you). Players choose a daily reminder time, or none, and nothing is sent at night (see 20.2).
  • §20.2 Never, 21:00 to 08:00
  • §20.2 Off 22:00 to 08:00 by default
  • §14.10 No win-back pressure. No escalating notifications, no "your islands miss you", no expiring comeback offers.
  • §30.5 Contextual notifications open at 14.4% versus 4.19% for generic. But one weekly push causes about 10% of users to disable notifications and three to six causes about 40%.
  • §17.8 This looks odd until you remember that a raid takes nothing: there is no harm to be protected from, and raids are anonymous while they happen.
  • §13 The defender is notified afterwards and can watch the replay.

Past a bucket the answer is 429 with Retry-After; the app says it is held back and its outbox retries later. Each edge isolate keeps its own buckets.

At the second epoch, is the extra slot a third law slot in the Heart, as §18.4 says, or a third crown slot, as §14.9's table says?

v3.6 states it both ways, and the two are different slots: a crown law works in every realm at double stability, and a slot in the Heart holds a law for the Heart alone. Epochs come after launch, so no launch work waits on it; it is here so the next version of the document says one thing.

What the build does today

Nothing: neither the server nor the client has epochs. TD.20 draws the Heart's two realm slots and the Spire's crown slots from the server, so either answer changes the server and not the screen. Screens v3 draws a third slot marked Locked in the Heart (D75's Heart row, screens_main.js:340); under A, that is the slot the second epoch opens after launch.

Recommended: A, A third law slot in the Heart (§18.4) medium confidence

Epochs are §18.4's to state, and §14.9's table sums them up, so the table follows the section. A grows one realm; B grows every realm at once, the larger reward, which you can still choose.

Also needed Nothing.
